To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of large, substrate adherent cells in cultures of human neural crest-derived neuroblastoma cells represents a differentiation of neuroblasts into cells with glial characteristics.

human neuroblastoma clones composed exclusively of N-type cells do not produce detectable amounts of collagen, while clones composed exclusively of large, substrate adherent cells (S-type) produce large amounts of type I and type III colla-gens.

human neuroblastoma clones with N-type or S-type morphology produce different amounts of collagen, and that the absence of secretion of alpha 2(I)-collagen is correlated with the presence of S- type cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the differentiation of human neuroblastomas, a malignant tumor of neural crest cells, into Schwann cell-like cells.
the characterization of the morphological and biochemical heterogeneity of human neuroblastomas.
a new model of human neuroblastomas, composed of two distinct types of cells, the N-type neuroblasts, and the S-type Schwann cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the S-type cell is a glial cell, and that the N-type cell is a neural cell, both derived from a common neural crest cell.
the neuroblastoma cell lines are a heterogeneous mixture of cells, and the presence of S cells represents a glial differentiation of neuroblastoma cell clones.

the presence of a high proportion of S-type cells is correlated to a high collagen secretion, whereas the presence of a large number of N-type cells is correlated with a low level of collagen secretion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neuroblastoma cell is capable of producing both neural and glial cell phenotypes.
the neuroblastoma cells are capable of producing type I and III collagen and that the production of these collagen types is regulated by the differentiation state of the neuroblastoma cell.
the S-type cells are a differentiated phenotype, while the N-type cells are a more primitive, undifferentiated phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neuroblastoma cells can differentiate along two distinct pathways, either neuroblastic or Schwannian.

human neuroblastoma clones composed exclusively of N-type cells can be used to study neuroblastoma biology and that the presence of cells with S morphology does not necessarily indicate the presence of Schwann cells.
the proportion of cells of the neuroblastoma cell cultures with S-type morphology is directly related to the amount of collagen produced by these cells.
